title: Stridor and upper airway obstruction

header.contentArea: Airway emergencies: stridor and upper airway obstruction in an inpatient
guidelineVersions: Resuscitation Council UK, The ABCDE Approach (published October 2015, last updated July 2024)
Resuscitation Council UK, Emergency Treatment of Anaphylaxis (published May 2021)

related.why: The larynx and emergency front-of-neck airway, needed if obstruction becomes complete
Anaphylaxis in theatre after induction, the same time-critical cause of airway obstruction seen here on the ward

brief.role: Surgical trainee reviewing a deteriorating inpatient
brief.scenario: Mrs Amelia Thornbury, 61, has noisy breathing, hoarseness and increasing work of breathing.
brief.task: Recognise upper airway obstruction and describe your immediate management as the examiner questions you.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Stridor means significant obstruction until proven otherwise, and it can worsen abruptly.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Waiting for complete obstruction, or for her saturations to fall, before calling for help.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd treat this as significant upper airway obstruction and not leave her alone."

flow: Keep her calm, avoid provoking deterioration

grid.label: Recognise stridor as significant obstruction (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Treats stridor as a minor noise or simple wheeze and continues routine review.
grid.pass: Recognises stridor as a sign of significant upper airway obstruction until proven otherwise and does not leave her alone.
grid.high: States that stridor and wheeze both suggest partial but significant obstruction, and escalates on the sound alone rather than waiting for desaturation.

grid.label: Immediate actions
grid.fail: Sends her for a routine chest X-ray before assessing or escalating.
grid.pass: Runs ABCDE, gives oxygen if hypoxaemic, and calls for senior anaesthetic/ENT/resuscitation help early while arranging definitive airway support.
grid.high: Prepares the space and team for difficult airway management in parallel with calling for help, rather than sequentially.

grid.label: Avoid provoking deterioration
grid.fail: Lies her flat or repeatedly examines the throat, provoking agitation.
grid.pass: Keeps her calm, avoids unnecessary agitation and repeated airway manipulation, and lets her find a comfortable position.
grid.high: Explains that agitation and lying flat can worsen a dynamic upper airway obstruction, so position and calm are part of treatment, not just observation.

grid.label: Differential by cause
grid.fail: Cannot list plausible causes beyond 'a chest problem'.
grid.pass: Lists causes: anaphylaxis or airway oedema, foreign body, tumour, infection, post-extubation oedema, trauma, vocal cord pathology.
grid.high: Prioritises the differential to what is actionable now — anaphylaxis and impending complete obstruction — rather than reciting the full list unordered.

grid.label: Treat anaphylaxis promptly if suspected (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Delays adrenaline while waiting for senior review in a patient with suspected anaphylaxis.
grid.pass: If anaphylaxis is suspected, gives IM adrenaline promptly following the Resuscitation Council algorithm rather than waiting.
grid.high: Gives 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh, and repeats after 5 minutes if there's no improvement.

grid.label: Anticipate abrupt deterioration
grid.fail: Waits for complete obstruction before calling anaesthetics.
grid.pass: Recognises that severe upper airway obstruction can deteriorate abruptly and escalates before complete obstruction develops.
grid.high: Sets a low threshold to call for a surgical airway team if there is any doubt, rather than waiting for exhaustion or a silent chest.

grid.label: Communicates the concern to the team
grid.fail: Does not tell nursing staff or document escalation triggers.
grid.pass: Clearly hands over the concern and escalation trigger to nursing staff and the team, documenting what to watch for.
grid.high: Agrees explicit criteria for immediate recall, such as any worsening stridor or desaturation, and confirms the escalation contact.

failures.move: Treating stridor as simple wheeze and continuing routine review.
failures.consequence: Delays recognition of a potentially rapidly fatal airway obstruction.

failures.move: Requesting a routine chest X-ray before escalating or assessing.
failures.consequence: Wastes time that could be used to call for definitive airway help.

failures.move: Waiting for senior review before giving adrenaline in suspected anaphylaxis.
failures.consequence: Delays a time-critical treatment in a rapidly deteriorating airway.

failures.move: Waiting for complete obstruction before calling anaesthetics.
failures.consequence: Loses the window to secure the airway before a crisis.

recovery.when: Asked why not just examine the throat yourself
recovery.line: Repeated examination can provoke agitation and worsen a dynamic obstruction; I'd rather call for help and keep her calm.

recovery.when: Asked to justify calling anaesthetics this early
recovery.line: Severe upper airway obstruction can deteriorate abruptly, so I'd rather call early than wait for a crisis.

knowledge.fact: Stridor or wheeze suggests partial but significant airway obstruction.
Causes include anaphylaxis/airway oedema, foreign body, tumour, infection, post-extubation oedema, trauma and vocal cord pathology.
Severe upper airway obstruction can deteriorate abruptly, so early escalation matters more than waiting for desaturation.
Suspected anaphylaxis: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed.

recall.think: Complete airway obstruction can develop abruptly.
recall.say: "Stridor: significant obstruction until proven otherwise — senior help now."
do: Keep her calm; avoid lying flat or repeated throat exam

numbers.value: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) IM adrenaline, repeat at 5 min

recall.trap: Waiting for complete obstruction or falling saturations before escalating.
recall.finish: Definitive airway management by the expert team; surgical airway if needed.

partner.opening: Mrs Thornbury, 61, is an inpatient with noisy breathing, hoarseness and increasing work of breathing. What does the stridor mean?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for observations or examines
reveals.finding: HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 92% on 2L oxygen, BP 148/88. Audible inspiratory stridor at rest, using accessory muscles, voice hoarse. No rash or facial swelling visible yet.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about recent history or exposures
reveals.finding: Had IV contrast for a CT two hours ago; new facial and lip swelling noted by the nurse in the last 10 minutes.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks to examine her face or skin
reveals.finding: Mild lip and periorbital swelling, no urticaria. No stridor at rest 10 minutes ago per the nursing notes — this is new.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for repeat observations after initial treatment
reveals.finding: SpO2 improves to 95% on oxygen; stridor persists but she is less agitated once sat upright.

push.question: Is this more concerning than a simple wheeze?
push.expect: Yes, stridor and wheeze both suggest partial but significant obstruction — treat as significant until proven otherwise.

push.question: What would you do right now, this minute?
push.expect: ABCDE, oxygen, call for senior anaesthetic/ENT/resuscitation help, arrange definitive airway support.

push.question: Would you examine her throat with a spatula to look?
push.expect: No — avoid unnecessary agitation or repeated airway manipulation; keep her calm.

push.question: Given the contrast and new facial swelling, what's your top concern?
push.expect: Anaphylaxis — give IM adrenaline promptly per the Resuscitation Council algorithm.

curveballs.prompt: She suddenly can't speak and looks exhausted.
curveballs.safeAnswer: This is critical deterioration — call for immediate expert airway help and prepare for definitive or surgical airway management.

curveballs.prompt: The registrar says to just observe for now since she's still talking.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Escalate anyway — stridor with increasing work of breathing needs senior review now, not observation alone.

curveballs.prompt: A nurse asks if she should lie the patient flat to make her more comfortable.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — keep her sitting up in a position she finds comfortable; lying flat can worsen the obstruction.

curveballs.prompt: There's no rash, so is anaphylaxis excluded?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — angioedema and airway symptoms can occur without a rash; treat on the overall picture.
